Stated Claim / Post Context:
Architect of California voting lawsuit to be disqualified as top federal prosecutor

The top federal prosecutor in Los Angeles, who led the Trump administration’s bid to block thousands of California voters, will be disqualified from his post on Nov. 23

Actual Article Body:
By Ajani Stella

November 17, 2026

to see more of our voting rights news coverage when you search.

The top federal prosecutor in Los Angeles, who led the Trump administration’s bid to block thousands of California voters, will be disqualified from his post on Nov. 23 after a federal judge declined Monday to suspend his earlier conclusion that the prosecutor was acting illegitimately.

In October, U.S. District Judge Michael Seabright ruled that Bill Essayli, the first assistant U.S. attorney for the Central District of California, had been “unlawfully serving as a ‘de facto’ United States Attorney.” That same month, Essayli spearheaded President Donald Trump’s unsuccessful effort to force California to segregate 20,000 ballots the administration claimed without evidence were cast by noncitizens.

Now, on Monday, Essayli will be blocked from fulfilling the U.S. attorney’s duties and overseeing two ongoing criminal prosecutions.

Essalyi’s appointment amounted to “unlawful attempts to appoint a de facto United States Attorney,” Seabright wrote.

Join 350,000 readers who rely on our daily and weekly newsletters for the latest in voting, elections and democracy.

The Justice Department appointed Essayli as interim U.S. attorney in April 2025, but he could legally only hold the position for 120 days. When his appointment lapsed, he became a special attorney and first assistant U.S. attorney — and kept leading the office illegally.

The Trump administration has repeatedly tried to circumvent congressional approval for U.S. attorneys across the country. Federal judges ruled that Alina Habba of New Jersey and John Sarcone of upstate New York were also unlawfully leading their offices.

In August, the 9th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals ruled that Sigal Chattah could not continue to run Nevada’s office without congressional approval. Seabright cited the 9th Circuit’s decision in his ruling against Essayli.

Essayli’s appeal to the 9th Circuit is currently pending, but Seabright’s Monday decision denied the government’s request to stay his ruling until the appellate court decides the case.

When Seabright’s October ruling came down, Essayli defended himself on social media and pledged to fight the decision.

“The Supreme Court will ultimately decide this matter,” Essayli wrote.
